--- title: "Regularisation" description: "A penalty on the size of the coefficients stops a model following noise. Ridge regression shrinks every coefficient, and the lasso sets some to exactly zero, but the inputs the lasso keeps are not a finding." order: 5 categories: [generalisation, tuning] --- ## Adding a little bias on purpose [The bias–variance trade-off](bias-variance.qmd) found that a random forest cuts variance by averaging many trees. Regularisation cuts it another way. It charges the model for large coefficients, so the model fits its own data a little worse, and new data better. This page introduces the two penalties in common use, ridge regression and the lasso, and shows that they can rescue a regression swamped by useless inputs. It also shows what the lasso's choice of inputs can and cannot tell you. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the data on this page The coastal survey used here is **simulated**, not a real survey. That is deliberate: because we wrote the generating process (`R/make-example-data.R`), we know the true relationships and can show whether a model recovers them. No real survey is being misrepresented, and the figures are not results about any real species. See `data/README.md` for what is built into it. ::: ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## About the Python tabs Most code blocks on this page have an **R** and a **Python** tab, and picking one switches the whole page. Both run when the site is built, and each tab shows its own output. The Python tab is the scikit-learn equivalent of the R; the figures come from R throughout, and a few steps with no scikit-learn counterpart have no Python tab, which is itself worth noticing. Expect the **numbers to differ slightly** where randomness is involved: R and Python draw their random splits from different generators, so the split is not the same one. The conclusions are. ::: ## A penalty on the size of the coefficients Least squares chooses the coefficients that make the squared error on the data as small as possible, and looks at nothing else. Regularisation adds a second term, a **penalty** that grows with the size of the coefficients, and minimises the two together: $$\text{squared error} + \lambda \times \text{penalty}$$ The weight λ (lambda) sets how hard the penalty pulls. With λ at zero the model is plain least squares, the most flexible it can be. As λ grows, the coefficients are pulled towards zero, and with a large enough λ every coefficient is zero and the model predicts the average. λ is a complexity setting, like a tree's node size: raising it adds bias and removes variance. Two penalties are in common use: - **Ridge regression** charges the sum of the squared coefficients. [Priors and ridge regression](../04-how-algorithms-learn/map-and-priors.qmd) derived it from a Normal prior. A squared penalty is heavy on large coefficients and light on small ones, so it shrinks every coefficient but sets none to exactly zero. - **The lasso** charges the sum of their absolute values, which the same page derived from a Laplace prior. The price of each unit is the same all the way down to zero, so a small coefficient that does little for the fit is cheaper to drop than to keep. The lasso sets such coefficients to exactly zero, and the input is gone from the model. **Elastic net** charges a mixture of the two. In tidymodels, `mixture` sets the share: 0 is ridge, 1 is the lasso. ::: {.diagram} ![Least squares fits the stations as closely as it can. Ridge regression shrinks every coefficient and sets none to zero. The lasso shrinks them too, and sets the small ones to exactly zero, which drops their inputs. The weight λ runs from least squares at zero to predicting the average when it is large.](img/regularisation.svg){fig-alt="Three cards, each with six coefficient bars about a zero line. Least squares, no penalty: bars of different heights. Ridge regression, squared penalty: every bar shorter than its least-squares outline, none at zero. Lasso, absolute penalty: the three large bars shorter, the three small ones exactly zero and drawn as open circles, so those inputs are dropped. Below, a card says the weight lambda sets how hard the penalty pulls, from lambda equals zero, least squares and the most flexible, to a large lambda, where every coefficient is zero and the model predicts the average. Raising lambda adds bias and removes variance. A note says to standardise the inputs first, because the penalty is charged per unit of each input."} ::: Both penalties add up coefficients, and a coefficient's size depends on the units of its input: an effect per metre of depth is a thousand times one per millimetre. The inputs are therefore standardised before a penalised fit, so that the penalty treats each one alike. ## Worked example [Model complexity](model-complexity.qmd) added columns of random numbers to a linear regression on the four measured inputs, and every column made it worse on new sites. Here the regression gets the first 200 of those random columns, and the penalties have to hold them back. The splits are those of the earlier pages: 20 random splits of the training sites into fitting sites and new sites, with each error averaged over the 20. ### Preparing the data ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean() split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75) train <- training(split) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splits <- group_mc_cv(train, group = site_id, prop = 0.75, times = 20) measured <- c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu") # the first 200 of Model complexity's random columns noise <- matrix(rnorm(nrow(train) * 460), nrow = nrow(train), dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("noise", 1:460)))[, 1:200] noise_columns <- bind_cols(select(train, station_id), as_tibble(noise)) inputs <- c(measured, colnames(noise)) # impute, then standardise, so the penalty treats every input alike inputs_recipe <- function(data, columns) { recipe(abundance ~ ., data = data[c("abundance", columns)]) |> step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |> step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors()) } ``` ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import pandas as pd from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNet, Lasso, LinearRegression, Ridge from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error from sklearn.model_selection import GroupShuffleSplit from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean survey = load_coastal_survey_clean() grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey, groups=survey["site_id"])) train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True) # 20 random splits of the training sites: fitting sites and new sites splitter = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=20, train_size=0.75, random_state=123) splits = list(splitter.split(train, groups=train["site_id"])) measured = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"] # the first 200 of Model complexity's random columns rng = np.random.default_rng(123) noise = pd.DataFrame(rng.standard_normal((len(train), 460))[:, :200], columns=[f"noise{i}" for i in range(1, 201)]) data = pd.concat([train, noise], axis=1) inputs = measured + list(noise.columns) # impute, then standardise, so the penalty treats every input alike def inputs_pipeline(model): return Pipeline([("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")), ("standardise", StandardScaler()), ("model", model)]) ``` ::: ::: ### Sweeping the penalty For each split, ridge regression, the lasso and an elastic net with `mixture = 0.5` are fitted to all 204 inputs, and each is scored on the new sites at 61 values of λ. Three models without a penalty set the scale: the regression on all 204 inputs, the regression on the four measured inputs alone, and predicting the fitting stations' average. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lambdas <- 10^seq(-3, 3, length.out = 61) # glmnet fits every λ in one go; predict() then picks one penalised_model <- function(mixture) { linear_reg(penalty = 1, mixture = mixture) |> set_engine("glmnet", path_values = lambdas) } score_split <- function(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) |> left_join(noise_columns, by = "station_id") new <- assessment(s) |> left_join(noise_columns, by = "station_id") error_on_new <- function(fitted, ...) { rmse_vec(new$abundance, predict(fitted, new, ...)$.pred) } fit_to <- function(columns, model) { workflow(inputs_recipe(fitting, columns), model) |> fit(fitting[c("abundance", columns)]) } penalised <- map(c(`Ridge regression` = 0, Lasso = 1, `Elastic net` = 0.5), \(m) { fitted <- fit_to(inputs, penalised_model(m)) tibble(lambda = lambdas, new = map_dbl(lambdas, \(l) error_on_new(fitted, penalty = l))) }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "model") unpenalised <- tibble( model = c("Linear regression, all inputs", "Linear regression, measured only", "predict the average"), new = c(error_on_new(fit_to(inputs, linear_reg())), error_on_new(fit_to(measured, linear_reg())), rmse_vec(new$abundance, rep(mean(fitting$abundance), nrow(new))))) bind_rows(penalised, unpenalised) } sweep <- map(splits$splits, score_split) |> list_rbind() |> group_by(model, lambda) |> summarise(new = mean(new), .groups = "drop") best <- sweep |> group_by(model) |> slice_min(new) |> ungroup() |> arrange(new) best |> mutate(lambda = signif(lambda, 2), new = round(new, 2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|model | lambda| new| |:--------------------------------|------:|----:| |Elastic net | 0.79| 4.55| |Lasso | 0.40| 4.55| |Linear regression, measured only | NA| 4.56| |Ridge regression | 20.00| 4.74| |predict the average | NA| 4.83| |Linear regression, all inputs | NA| 6.41|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} lambdas = 10 ** np.linspace(-3, 3, 61) # scikit-learn's Ridge puts no 1/n in front of the squared error, as glmnet # does, so its alpha is λ times the number of stations penalised = { "Ridge regression": lambda lam, n: Ridge(alpha=lam * n), "Lasso": lambda lam, n: Lasso(alpha=lam), "Elastic net": lambda lam, n: ElasticNet(alpha=lam, l1_ratio=0.5), } def error_on_new(fitted, new, columns): return root_mean_squared_error(new["abundance"], fitted.predict(new[columns])) rows = [] for fitting_rows, new_rows in splits: fitting, new = data.iloc[fitting_rows], data.iloc[new_rows] for name, make in penalised.items(): for lam in lambdas: fitted = inputs_pipeline(make(lam, len(fitting))).fit( fitting[inputs], fitting["abundance"]) rows.append({"model": name, "lambda": lam, "new": error_on_new(fitted, new, inputs)}) for name, columns in [("Linear regression, all inputs", inputs), ("Linear regression, measured only", measured)]: fitted = inputs_pipeline(LinearRegression()).fit( fitting[columns], fitting["abundance"]) rows.append({"model": name, "lambda": np.nan, "new": error_on_new(fitted, new, columns)}) average = np.repeat(fitting["abundance"].mean(), len(new)) rows.append({"model": "predict the average", "lambda": np.nan, "new": root_mean_squared_error(new["abundance"], average)}) sweep = (pd.DataFrame(rows) .groupby(["model", "lambda"], dropna=False, as_index=False)["new"].mean()) best = (sweep.loc[sweep.groupby("model")["new"].idxmin()] .sort_values("new").reset_index(drop=True)) best.round({"lambda": 3, "new": 2}) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | model | lambda | new | |:---------------------------------|---------:|------:| | Linear regression, measured only | nan | 4.31 | | Lasso | 0.398 | 4.37 | | Elastic net | 0.631 | 4.37 | | Ridge regression | 3.981 | 4.47 | | predict the average | nan | 4.53 | | Linear regression, all inputs | nan | 5.82 | ::: ::: ::: ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reference <- best |> filter(is.na(lambda)) |> # each label where no curve crosses it mutate(x = if_else(model == "Linear regression, all inputs", 1000, 0.001), hjust = if_else(model == "Linear regression, all inputs", 1, 0)) sweep |> filter(!is.na(lambda), model != "Elastic net") |> ggplot(aes(lambda, new, colour = model)) + geom_hline(data = reference, aes(yintercept = new), linetype = "dashed", colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_text(data = reference, aes(x = x, y = new, label = model, hjust = hjust), inherit.aes = FALSE, vjust = -0.5, size = 3.4, colour = ml_palette[["grey"]]) + geom_line(linewidth = 1) + scale_x_log10(breaks = 10^(-3:3), labels = scales::label_number(drop0trailing = TRUE, big.mark = ",")) + scale_colour_manual(values = c(`Ridge regression` = ml_palette[["blue"]], Lasso = ml_palette[["vermilion"]])) + labs(x = "λ (log scale)", y = "RMSE on new sites (individuals)", colour = NULL, title = "The lasso throws out the random columns; ridge only shrinks them") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Error on new sites against the penalty weight λ, for ridge regression and the lasso on the four measured inputs and 200 random columns, averaged over 20 splits of the training sites. The horizontal lines are the three models without a penalty.](regularisation_files/figure-html/fig-sweep-1.png){#fig-sweep fig-alt='Two curves of RMSE on new sites against lambda on a log scale from 0.001 to 1000. Both curves start on the left at a line for the regression on all inputs, at 6.41. The lasso curve falls to its lowest point, 4.55, near lambda 0.4, then rises to the average line and stays there. The ridge curve falls later and more slowly, to 4.74 near lambda 20, then creeps back up towards the average line. A dashed line for predicting the average sits at 4.83, and a line for the regression on the measured inputs alone at 4.56, level with the bottom of the lasso curve.' width=1400} ::: ::: ::: ### Two penalties against no penalty **Unchecked, the random columns cost dearly.** The regression on all 204 inputs has an error on new sites of 6.41, worse than predicting the average, 4.83. This is [Model complexity](model-complexity.qmd)'s finding again: each random column lets the regression follow a little more noise. **The penalty is a complexity setting.** Both curves start at that regression on the left, where λ is small, and head for the average on the right, where λ is so large that every coefficient is zero or close to it. The lowest error lies in between, as it did for a tree's node size on [Underfitting and overfitting](underfitting-and-overfitting.qmd). **The lasso did as well as knowing which columns were random.** At its best λ, the lasso scores 4.55, against 4.56 for a regression given only the four measured inputs. It got there by setting nearly all the random columns to zero. The elastic net lands close to the lasso, at a larger λ, since half its penalty is the lasso's. **Ridge regression helped less.** Its best error is 4.74. It keeps all 204 coefficients, yet does far better than least squares with the same 204: the penalty stops them moving freely, so counting coefficients no longer measures the model's complexity. But ridge only shrinks each random column, and 200 small coefficients still add up. Ridge suits data in which many inputs each matter a little; the lasso suits data in which a few matter and the rest are noise, as here. The best λ was chosen by the same errors the table reports, which flatters it a little. [Hyperparameter selection](hyperparameter-selection.qmd) shows how to choose a setting such as λ and still get an honest error. ### The inputs the lasso kept It is tempting to read the inputs the lasso keeps as the ones that matter. Here we know which columns are random, so we can check. The lasso is fitted to each split's fitting stations again at its best λ, and each kept input is counted. ::: {.panel-tabset group="language"} ## R ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} kept <- map(splits$splits, \(s) { fitting <- analysis(s) |> left_join(noise_columns, by = "station_id") workflow(inputs_recipe(fitting, inputs), penalised_model(1)) |> fit(fitting[c("abundance", inputs)]) |> tidy(penalty = lasso_lambda) |> filter(term != "(Intercept)", estimate != 0) }) |> list_rbind(names_to = "split") kept |> count(term, name = "splits", sort = TRUE) |> head(8) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
|term | splits| |:-----------------|------:| |chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 20| |depth_m | 20| |noise68 | 19| |noise102 | 16| |noise192 | 15| |noise87 | 14| |noise153 | 13| |noise32 | 12|
::: ::: ## Python ::: {.cell} ```{.python .cell-code} lasso_lambda = best.loc[best["model"] == "Lasso", "lambda"].item() kept = [] for split_number, (fitting_rows, new_rows) in enumerate(splits): fitting = data.iloc[fitting_rows] fitted = inputs_pipeline(Lasso(alpha=lasso_lambda)).fit( fitting[inputs], fitting["abundance"]) coefficients = fitted.named_steps["model"].coef_ kept += [{"split": split_number, "term": term} for term, b in zip(inputs, coefficients) if b != 0] kept = pd.DataFrame(kept) (kept["term"].value_counts().rename("splits").rename_axis("term") .reset_index().head(8)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} | term | splits | |:------------------|---------:| | chlorophyll_mg_m3 | 20 | | noise149 | 18 | | depth_m | 16 | | noise39 | 15 | | noise120 | 15 | | noise29 | 10 | | noise98 | 8 | | noise180 | 7 | ::: ::: ::: **The lasso kept random columns.** On average it kept nine random columns per split, and 50 different ones across the 20. One of them, noise68, was kept in 19 of the 20 splits, almost as often as depth and chlorophyll. The splits share most of their sites, so a chance match between a random column and the counts at those sites turns up again and again. Keeping an input, even in split after split, does not show that it matters. **The lasso dropped measured inputs.** It kept depth and chlorophyll in every split, and dropped temperature and salinity in every one. Dropping an input does not show that it is useless either. Temperature falls with depth on this shelf (their correlation is −0.46), so once depth is in the model, temperature adds little that depth has not already said, and the lasso drops whichever of the pair helps less. The lasso is a way to predict well from many inputs. Its list of inputs is one draw from the data, and a different set of stations would give a different list. ## Key points ::: {.key-points} - Regularisation adds a penalty on the size of the coefficients, weighted by λ. Raising λ adds bias and removes variance; λ is a complexity setting, chosen on new data. - Ridge regression charges the squared coefficients and shrinks them all; the lasso charges their absolute values and sets some to exactly zero. Elastic net mixes the two. - Standardise the inputs first, so the penalty treats each one alike. - With 200 random columns among its inputs, the lasso predicted about as well as a regression told which inputs were measured, and ridge regression less well. - The lasso kept some random columns and dropped some measured inputs. Its list of inputs is not evidence of which ones matter. ::: ## Try it yourself 1. Give the regression 50 random columns instead of 200, with `[, 1:50]` in place of `[, 1:200]`. Does the lasso still beat ridge regression by as much? 2. Remove `"depth_m"` from `measured` and rerun the sweep and the count. Does the lasso now keep temperature?
